Case study 01
AI Product · Data-rich UI · Content Systems · Birdeye

The tooltips shipped broken. I went through three doors to fix them, then pushed the changes to the codebase myself.

Lead Content Designer · Search AI dashboard · Tooltip revamp · 2025 to 2026

40+
Tooltip strings audited, rewritten, and pushed directly to the GitHub repo via a reviewed PR.
3
Competitors analyzed: Profound, Peec AI, and Semrush. Pattern pulled from all three, gaps identified in ours.
$1M
Quarterly revenue at launch. CPO called it the fastest-selling Birdeye product. Content system cited directly.
How it started

PMs and devs dropped tooltips into the codebase at runtime. Nobody reviewed them.

Search AI launched under a 3-month deadline. The dashboard shows metrics most business owners had never seen before: visibility score, share of voice, citation share, average position. These are not standard analytics terms. People arrived with no frame of reference for what they were looking at.

In the rush to ship, tooltip strings were added by PMs and developers directly at runtime. Nobody flagged them for content review. Some were grammatically broken. Some described the metric using the metric's own name. Most percentage-based metrics never explained what the denominator was. A 50% visibility score out of what? That distinction changes the number significantly, and we were not explaining it.

I spotted the pattern, documented the scope, and got PM buy-in to fix it. Then I went to the engineering lead. He redirected me to a developer on the team. The developer said no: he could not pull every tooltip string from the codebase, it would take too long to locate them all.

I showed him how to use Claude to do it. He came around. We got the full set of tooltip strings extracted from the codebase in one session.

The research

I studied how Profound, Peec AI, and Semrush explained the same metrics.

I went through each competitor's dashboard and documented how they wrote tooltips for the same metrics we were showing. Profound had the strongest system: every percentage metric used a worked example with the calculation shown, and the denominator was always explicit. Peec AI kept tooltips short but always included a directional note (lower is better, higher is better). Semrush relied more on linked documentation than inline explanations.

Four things I pulled from the analysis and applied to ours: worked examples with real numbers for every percentage metric, context before the formula for non-obvious calculations like share of voice, caveats where calculation scope could confuse (rank only calculated among top 50 brands), and no filler openers like Shows, Indicates, Displays, or Tracks.

The tooltip map: current copy, revised copy, status (Ready / On hold), and dev notes for every string across the dashboard.
From my Profound analysis

These are the actual screenshots I studied.

Profound's tooltip approach: plain definition + worked example. Visibility score tooltip visible on hover.
Visibility Score Rank and Share of Voice tooltips. Note how SoV explains why 100 responses can produce 500 brand mentions before showing the formula.
Average Position tooltip and the full Prompts table. The rank tooltip adds a caveat: calculated only among top 50 most visible brands.
Three rewrites that show the pattern
Visibility score, before

How often your brand appears, in AI-generated answers. For example, your brand is mentioned in 50 responses out of a total of 100 tracked, the visibility score will be 50%.

Visibility score, after

The percentage of AI responses that mention your brand. For example, if AI mentions your brand in 50 out of 100 tracked responses, your visibility score is 50%.

What changed: Rogue comma removed. Passive description replaced with a direct definition. Example tightened without losing meaning. Consistent with every other percentage metric on the dashboard.

Share of voice, before

The percentage of AI-generated answers in which your brand is mentioned compared to the total mentions of all tracked brands.

Share of voice, after

Your brand's share of all brand mentions across AI responses. Each response can mention multiple brands. For example, if there are 500 total brand mentions across 100 responses and your brand accounts for 50, your share of voice is 10% (50/500).

What changed: Added the context that one response can mention multiple brands. Without that, the 10% figure makes no sense. The original forced users to do math they did not have the setup for.

Sentiment score, before

The percentage of AI-generated answers that portray your brand positively. A higher score indicates more favorable mentions across AI sites.

Sentiment score, after

The percentage of claims about your brand in AI answers that are positive. Each AI response can contain multiple claims. This metric tracks how many of those claims carry a positive tone.

What changed: The original implied sentiment equals percentage of responses. It is actually percentage of claims. One response can contain multiple claims. Someone seeing 84% would assume 84% of responses are positive, which is not how it works.

Before: Indicates whether this page mentions your business. Filler opener, no context.
After: Whether this page mentions your business in the AI-generated answer. Direct, no filler.
How I pushed the changes

I cloned the repo, edited the string files, and raised a PR.

Once the revised copy was reviewed and signed off by the PM and design team, I got access to the GitHub repository. I cloned it locally, located the tooltip string files in the codebase, made the edits directly, and raised a pull request. The PR included a line-by-line breakdown of what changed and why for each string, so the engineer reviewing it could approve without needing to chase me for context.

The tooltip map spreadsheet I produced covered every metric across Settings, Reports (Prompt, Platforms, Sentiment, Accuracy, Ranking, Visibility, Citations), Overview, and Website Analytics. Each row had the original string, the revised string, a status (Ready or On hold), and a dev note. On-hold items flagged metric definitions that needed data team confirmation before copy could be written. Shipping wrong copy about a metric is worse than shipping no copy.

Case study 02
Mobile · iOS · Prototyping · Content + Design · Birdeye

I volunteered for a mobile feature nobody asked me to touch. Built the prototype myself in Xcode to get engineers and PM on the same page.

Lead Content Designer · Birdeye Mobile Ticketing · iOS · 2026

Voluntary
No one assigned this to me. I spotted content and design problems in the ticketing feature and knocked on every door to get involved.
Xcode
Built an interactive SwiftUI prototype from scratch using the mobile design system tokens to show decisions in context, not just describe them.
Shipped
Content revamped across the full feature. Design decisions adopted. PM and engineering buy-in secured through live prototype walkthroughs.
How it started

I looked at the ticketing feature and saw problems nobody had flagged.

I came across the Birdeye mobile ticketing feature while doing a routine product review. What I found was a content and design audit's worth of problems sitting in a shipped feature: status labels using color codes the design language did not support, source pills with inconsistent treatment (some outlined, some plain text, some with icons), Cancel as a back affordance on screens where nothing had been edited, an empty activity state sitting at the top of a tall screen with no centering, and a watching status filter written in first-person sentences instead of attributes.

None of this was my responsibility. I was not assigned to mobile. But I documented everything I saw, wrote up the problems with reasoning, and went to the PM to make the case for fixing it.

The prototype

Words on a slide were not going to be enough. I built the thing in Xcode.

To get genuine buy-in from engineering and PM, I needed to show the decisions working in context, not describe them in a document. I got access to the mobile repository, cloned it locally, and built an interactive SwiftUI prototype.

The mobile design system was not fully set up for the feature. I learned to extract the design tokens manually from the existing codebase, mapped them to the components I needed, and used them throughout the prototype so it matched the real product. I built multiple versions across several iterations, walking through each one with engineers on the same call and taking feedback in real time.

Content and design audit notes alongside the live screens
Detail screen: Watchers multi-select, activity log, tag management
SwiftUI prototype built in Xcode using extracted design system tokens
Source filter and Watching Status screens with UXW notes
Key content decisions

Every label was a deliberate call, not a default.

Watchers label logic. 0 watchers shows No watchers. 1 watcher shows the person's name. More than 1 shows N watching. Simple label logic that removes ambiguity without adding UI complexity.

Cancel replaced with a proper back affordance. Cancel implies the user is discarding an edit. On screens where nothing has been edited, Cancel creates a false mental model. Replaced with a back arrow where no destructive action is possible.

Watching Status filter rewritten as attributes. The original used first-person sentences: I am watching, I am not watching. Filters are attributes, not statements. Changed to Watching and Not watching. Also flagged the title casing: Watching Status needed sentence case.

Others standardized to Other in the source list. Consistency call. The list had Social, Surveys, Reviews, Insights, Others. Others is a plural that breaks the pattern. Changed to Other.

CTA changed to View ticket. The original said View activities. The primary object is the ticket, not the activity log. The CTA should name what the user is going to see.

What made this different

Most content designers would have written a recommendation doc and handed it over. I built the prototype, showed up to engineering calls with something interactive, and iterated on the call. The result was not just better copy. It was a better designed feature, and it got there because I did not wait for someone to ask me to be involved.

Case study 03
AI Tools · Figma · Content Systems · Birdeye

I built a Figma plugin that reviews UX copy against the content system in real time, before anything leaves the file.

Lead Content Designer · Birdeye UXW Agent · Figma Plugin · 2025

EoTM
Employee of the Month at Birdeye, within 6 months of joining. Plugin cited as a direct reason by leadership.
Live
In active use inside Figma across the design team. Validates multiple text layers simultaneously.
AI
Uses AI to check copy against the content system. Explains what is wrong and why, not just flags it.
Birdeye UXW Agent plugin UI. Select text layers, pick component type, validate.
Plugin running on a real Figma file. Validation results appear inline next to the selected layers.
The problem

The feedback loop in Figma was slow and the problems were always found too late.

The standard content review process was: designer writes copy in Figma, hands off, content designer reviews, leaves comments, designer revises, repeat. By the time copy problems surfaced, the design was often already in engineering review. Fixing copy at that stage meant reopening files, updating strings, re-reviewing, sometimes delaying handoff.

I built the plugin to move that feedback to the earliest possible moment. The designer selects text layers, picks the component type, clicks Validate content. The plugin checks the copy against Birdeye's content system using AI and surfaces findings directly in the Figma canvas, next to the layers that need attention.

What it checks

Voice and tone compliance against Birdeye's content guidelines. Flags copy that drifts from the product's established tone.

AI tell-tale phrases like seamlessly, robust, leverage, ensure, transformative. These are banned from product copy.

Passive constructions in CTAs. A CTA that does not start with a verb fails. The plugin catches these and shows the relevant style guide rule.

Component-specific rules. A field label has different standards than an error message or an empty state. The component type dropdown lets the plugin apply the right rules for the right context.

The system behind it

The plugin is only as useful as the content rules it enforces. I wrote those rules, structured them for machine parsing, and kept them updated as the product voice evolved. The plugin is the interface. The content system is the substance. Both needed to be built and maintained by the same person to stay aligned.

Case study 04
AI Tools · Chrome Extension · Live Audit · Birdeye

I built a Chrome extension that audits UX writing quality on any live product page in one click.

Lead Content Designer · Birdeye Content Auditor · v0.2.0 · 2026

30s
What used to take an hour of manual page-by-page review now takes thirty seconds and produces an exportable report.
Score
UX Clarity Score from 0 to 100. Readability, grade level, passive voice, sentence length, style guide compliance.
Compare
Built-in competitor comparison. Audit Birdeye and a competitor, compare scores side by side. No extensions needed on both pages simultaneously.
Extension popup. One URL field, one button.
Audit running on birdeye.com. UX Clarity Score 97, findings broken down by signal.
Findings panel: CTA clarity score, passive voice count, style guide violations, empty states.
Benchmark comparison: Birdeye vs Cvent across 9 signals. Birdeye scores 0 passive voice, 78 CTAs vs Cvent's 62.
Compare tab. Birdeye baseline saved, competitor queued.
Same audit run on cvent.com for comparison.
Side-by-side view with competitor data loaded.
What it does

The extension extracts all visible product copy from a live page, filters out navigation, data tables, metrics, and noise, and runs it through a four-signal scoring engine: Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Passive Voice Rate, and Sentence Complexity. Each signal is weighted by its impact on product copy quality and combined into a single UX Clarity Score.

Beyond the score, it flags passive voice sentences verbatim, identifies long sentences with word counts, lists all CTAs on the page, and flags generic action labels. The export produces two files simultaneously: a structured JSON report for engineering handoff and a flat CSV for PMs to paste into Jira tickets.

The Compare tab lets me save a baseline audit for any site, then run the same audit on a competitor and compare scores across all nine signals side by side. This is how I track whether Birdeye's content quality is moving in the right direction over time, and where specific competitors are doing better.

What I built it on

Chrome Manifest V3 architecture with a content script, popup, and message passing layer. Scoring engine is entirely rule-based and runs client-side with no external dependencies. The repo is at github.com/rishisharma-tech/ux-communication-audit-extension. Built using Cursor and Claude as the engineering pair, with every major decision documented in Jira before implementation.

Case study 05
Payments · Compliance · Financial Terminology · Cvent

Two projects from Cvent where the language had to be accurate before it could be clear.

Lead Content Designer · Cvent Hospitality Cloud + Compliance Reporting · 2023 to 2024

🔒

Screenshots withheld. NDA-protected product work.

Project A: Hospitality Cloud payments

People were abandoning checkout because they could not tell if they were being charged once or every month.

Cvent Hospitality Cloud runs on a freemium model. Event organizers get 5 RFPs free. Hit the limit and a self-checkout upgrade flow kicks in. The copy on that payment screen mixed one-time and recurring signals. Nobody could tell if this was a subscription or a one-off. At the card screen, that ambiguity kills conversions.

I rewrote the subscription confirmation copy to name the plan, state the amount, confirm the cadence, and add a release valve in one sentence. Replaced an empty billing date field with a specific date and a 7-day reminder notice. Added multi-currency conversion notices with live rate disclaimers, working with the localization team across markets. Every terminology decision was run past product and legal before anything went to copy.

Down
Drop-off at payment confirmation after the rewrite.
5 RFPs
The PLG free limit that triggered the checkout upgrade flow.
Global
Multi-currency checkout. Worked with localization across markets.
Project B: SPP pharma compliance reporting

Four different labels for the same number was a compliance problem, not a style problem.

Pharma event managers use Cvent to track money spent on healthcare professionals across events. This is regulatory reporting: in many markets, those figures have to be publicly disclosed. The key metric, Spend Per Person, appeared across the product as SPP, spend per attendee, and per-person cost. Four labels for one number.

I standardized the terminology across labels, headers, config screens, and export column names, separated two admin workflows that were sitting on the same setup page with no distinction between them, and wrote inline guidance so pharma clients could answer setup questions without raising a support ticket. The compliance team reviewed every terminology decision before I applied it.

1
Term standardized across 4 surfaces. Locked to Spend Per Person and SPP.
2
Admin workflows separated and labeled on the same setup screen.
Down
Support load. Clients could self-serve setup answers without a ticket.
